| [THEORY-067](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-067.md) | Self-control over time needs no faculty of will: interests that dominate at different delays bargain, and resolve is the recursive staking of expected future choices on the present one | Ainslie's précis ([LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md)): hyperbolic discounting makes a smaller, sooner reward temporarily preferred, so successive "interests" conflict as in a repeated prisoner's dilemma. Treating a choice as a precedent bundles the series, and summed hyperbolic curves favour the larger, later rewards; a lapse costs credibility. Will is that recursion, not an organ. Schelling ([LIT-602](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-602.md)) describes the same divided chooser from the side of tactics: we manage our later selves as we manage other people. The mathematics of bundling is sound; that willpower works this way is argued, and the précis concedes it is hard to test directly. It is a claim about how control is achieved, not about whose control is self-governance. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-149](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-149.md) | Users can govern a shared resource durably without either privatisation or central control, and the institutions that last are marked not by particular rules but by structural regularities: user-made and user-monitored rules, graduated sanctions, cheap local conflict resolution, recognised rights to self-organise, and nested layers of governance | Ostrom's account, read in her Nobel lecture ([LIT-719](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-719.md)). Coded case meta-analyses, laboratory and field experiments and multi-country field studies agree that resource users often self-govern successfully. Long-surviving institutions share eight design principles that failed ones lack. The principles are correlates of survival, not tested causes, and their reach beyond common-pool resources is not shown. | Active |
| [THEORY-290](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-290.md) v2 | In a two-debater, three-proposition model of deductive debate whose payoff trades true beliefs against changes of mind, the most truth-conducive equilibrium can fall short of the truth-optimal profile because one debater free-rides on the other's belief-disrupting arguments, and in a narrow band of mixed equilibria a higher weight on truth gives lower equilibrium accuracy | Handfield, Garcia, Hilbe and Yeo (2025), [LIT-966](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-966.md), read in full in [NOTE-795](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-795.md). With payoff w·v − d (true beliefs against changes of mind), debate between two deductive reasoners is a cooperative dilemma at low and moderate truth weights. Typically one argues boldly and the other free-rides (a snowdrift), and at low weights both exit. A small dip in accuracy as w rises occurs in a narrow band of mixed equilibria. It is shown numerically for two players and three propositions. It concerns collective accuracy, not a belief the pair settles on, and at high truth weight in short debates there is no dilemma. The title claims the model only; groups and richer strategies are QUESTION-173. | Active |
| [THEORY-404](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-404.md) v2 | With a common prior, a sender who commits to a signal the receiver observes can induce any distribution of posteriors whose mean is the prior, so an openly designed experiment moves a fully informed Bayesian receiver whenever the concave closure of the sender's value lies above its value at the prior; at the optimum, under the paper's tie-breaking, the receiver is certain when she takes the sender's worst action and indifferent when she takes another | Kamenica & Gentzkow (2011), [LIT-1021](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1021.md), read in [NOTE-717](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-717.md) with the proofs. | [THEORY-414](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-414.md) | Institutions are rules in equilibrium, correlated equilibria of coordination games with several equilibria that the players represent to themselves as rules, and a constitutive rule 'X counts as Y in C' is a regulative rule split by a coined term into a base rule and a status rule, so the term adds a name and cognitive economy but no new kind of fact | Hindriks & Guala (2015, online 2014), [LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md), read with the authors' reply to six commentators in [NOTE-395](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-395.md). | [THEORY-437](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-437.md) | When each agent's feasible actions depend on the others' actions, an equilibrium exists if every action set is a contractible polyhedron, every constraint correspondence has a closed graph with non-empty compact values, payoffs and the maximum-value functions are continuous, and every best-response set is contractible; convexity is not needed | Debreu (1952), [LIT-067](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-067.md), read in full in [NOTE-037](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-037.md). | [THEORY-457](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-457.md) | When people can choose their cooperation partners and have equal outside options, the stable division of jointly produced gains is in proportion to each partner's contribution, and partner choice selects for a genuine sense of fairness as proportionality | Baumard, André & Sperber (2013), [LIT-508](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-508.md), read in [NOTE-407](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-407.md), with its 28 commentaries and Response. | [THEORY-466](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-466.md) | Among contestants of equal prowess with dangerous weapons, individual selection can favour conventional fighting backed by retaliation: an escalating Hawk is not evolutionarily stable, Retaliator is at most neutrally stable because Mouse ties it, and in a contest settled by persistence alone no fixed persistence is stable while an exponential mixture is | Maynard Smith & Price (1973), [LIT-505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-505.md), read in full in [NOTE-404](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-404.md). | [THEORY-468](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-468.md) | Morality is the set of solutions to recurrent problems of cooperation, so each of the seven cooperation problems game theory identifies yields a moral domain valued in every culture, and behaviour unrelated to cooperation is morally neutral | Curry (2016), [LIT-503](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-503.md), read in [NOTE-408](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-408.md), with its two tests, [LIT-047](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-047.md) ([NOTE-034](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-034.md)) and [LIT-496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-496.md) ([NOTE-412](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-412.md)). | [THEORY-567](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-567.md) | In the donation game, where a cooperator pays c for another to get b, defectors win in a well-mixed population, and each of five mechanisms makes cooperators evolutionarily stable above a benefit-to-cost threshold: kin selection r > c/b, direct reciprocity w > c/b, indirect reciprocity q > c/b, network reciprocity b/c > k and group selection b/c > 1 + n/m; the rules cover altruism only, not mutualism, coordination or conflict | Nowak (2006), [LIT-501](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-501.md), read in [NOTE-409](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-409.md), main text only. | [THEORY-672](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-672.md) | In the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma with a probability w of meeting again, no strategy does better against an established TIT FOR TAT than TIT FOR TAT does against itself if and only if w ≥ (T−R)/(T−P) and w ≥ (T−R)/(R−S); always defecting is stable for every w, a cluster of reciprocators can invade it, and a nice stable strategy resists clusters, but the stability is only neutral, since always cooperating ties | Axelrod & Hamilton (1981), [LIT-498](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-498.md), read in full in [NOTE-411](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-411.md). | [THEORY-835](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-835.md) | When two firms each hire the best available candidate by a noisy ranking, and the ranking model makes an independent re-ranking worth more to the second mover than its own next choice and makes a weaker first mover better for it, then for every accuracy of the private rankings there is a more accurate shared algorithmic ranking that each firm strictly prefers to use whatever the other does, and with which both firms, and total welfare, do worse than if neither used it | Kleinberg and Raghavan (2021), [LIT-1326](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1326.md), read in [NOTE-1033](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1033.md). | [THEORY-936](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-936.md) | In two-agent rock–scissors–paper played by softmax reinforcement learners, nonzero tie rewards give quasiperiodic tori and Hamiltonian chaos without memory decay, and limit cycles and chaotic attractors with it, over a large share of the tie-reward range simulated | Sato & Crutchfield (arXiv 2002; PRE 2003), [LIT-1520](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1520.md), read in full in [NOTE-1144](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1144.md), pp. 2–3 and Figs. 1–3. Numerical results for one game, two agents and the parameters shown; the zero-decay, zero-sum case was first reported in Sato, Akiyama and Farmer (PNAS 2002), which is not held. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-938](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-938.md) | Cross learning has the expected motion of the replicator dynamic and follows it on any finite horizon in the continuous-time limit, but for every learning speed the discrete process converges with probability one to a pure strategy profile, even in games where the replicator dynamic cycles | Börgers & Sarin (JET 1997; working paper 1993), [LIT-1505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1505.md), read in full from the 1995 working paper in [NOTE-1149](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1149.md). Two players running Cross's rule with payoffs in (0, 1): expected change equals the discrete replicator step (Proposition 3); the slow-learning limit is the Taylor replicator dynamic at each finite time (Proposition 4); for every step size the process is absorbed in a pure profile with probability one (Proposition 5). The equivalence is pointwise in time, not uniform. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-939](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-939.md) | In a multi-agent system run against a world utility, a private utility is factored, ranking each agent's own alternatives with the others fixed as the world utility ranks them, exactly when it is an increasing function of the world utility given the components the agent cannot affect; the world utility minus its value with the agent's effect set clamped is factored, and in a sixty-agent bar problem clamping to the average action learned better than clamping to absence or using the world utility itself | Wolpert & Tumer's NASA report ([LIT-1506](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1506.md)), read in full in NOTE- tmpo0w02 because their Advances in Complex Systems paper ([LIT-1515](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1515.md)) could not be reached. The characterisation is stated with its proof deferred; the "if" half and the WLU's factoredness were checked when filed. Factoredness is ordinal, member by member, and needs no scale shared among members. The WLU is not a causal counterfactual: it re- scores the actual history with one member's part replaced. Removal was not the best clamp. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-940](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-940.md) | In a finite symmetric zero-sum game, successive Nash clusters are weakly ordered by relative population performance, and a strategy that beats every member of a population containing a whole cluster lies in a strictly earlier cluster | Czarnecki et al. (2020), [LIT-1504](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1504.md), Definition 3 and Theorems 2–3, read from arXiv v2 in [NOTE-1146](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1146.md), proofs followed and re-derived. RPP is the population value of Balduzzi et al. (2019), [LIT-1509](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1509.md). It holds for any Nash clustering of any finite symmetric zero-sum game and does not depend on the spinning-top hypothesis. The order is weak, since clusters can tie, and cardinal, since RPP uses payoff magnitudes. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-941](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-941.md) | If every player of a finite game switches from its last action to each other action with probability proportional to its positive conditional regret, the empirical distribution of play converges almost surely to the set of correlated equilibria | Hart & Mas-Colell (Econometrica 2000; handout 1996), [LIT-1521](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1521.md), read in full in [NOTE-1142](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1142.md). Convergence is of time-averaged joint frequencies to a set, not of play to an equilibrium; the common history is the correlating device; inertia is needed; and interior correlated equilibria that are not pure Nash cannot be the limit. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-942](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-942.md) | The α-Rank chain over pure strategy profiles, built from Fermi-imitation fixation probabilities in finite populations with rare mutation, has a unique stationary distribution at every finite ranking intensity; as the intensity grows without bound its transitions become those of Markov chains confined to the sink strongly connected components of the game's weakly-better-response graph, each of which lies inside a single chain component of the replicator flow | Omidshafiei et al. (2019), [LIT-1516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1516.md), Theorems 2.1.2, 2.4.24 and 2.5.1, read from arXiv v4 in [NOTE-1156](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1156.md), proofs followed. Irreducibility is immediate, and the α → ∞ limit is of transition matrices. The link to the replicator flow rests on a volume-preservation step that is asserted, not carried out. Not shown: what the stationary distribution tends to, how it splits among several sinks, or invariance to duplicated strategies, which the reader found it lacks. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-943](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-943.md) | When a center with no ground truth pays each rater a strictly proper scoring rule on the distribution of a reference rater's report implied by her own report, under a common prior and a known signal model in which raters' signals are stochastically relevant to one another, truthful reporting is a strict Nash equilibrium, but not the only one: equilibria in which every rater reports the same signal regardless of what she observed also exist | Miller, Resnick and Zeckhauser's Proposition 1, read in full in [NOTE-1139](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1139.md) from the January 2005 draft, with the proof and the worked example (p(H) = .5, f(h \| H) = .85, f(h \| L) = .45; honest l scores −0.69, false h −0.75 under the log rule) re-derived. The same example has two uninformative equilibria, which the authors set aside as not focal. The scheme replaces ground truth with the center's model of how honest signals correlate. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-944](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-944.md) | The value of the zero-sum game between two populations' evaluation matrices does not depend on which Nash equilibrium is used, is unchanged by adding agents that behave as mixtures of existing members, and is not positive for a population whose agents are all behavioural mixtures of the other's | Balduzzi et al. (2019), [LIT-1509](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1509.md), Propositions 2 and 5, read from arXiv v2 in [NOTE-1143](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1143.md), proofs followed and re-derived. Relative population performance is a game value, so equilibrium selection never arises. Behaviourally redundant members leave it unchanged, and a population contained in another's behavioural hull cannot beat it. It scores populations, not members, it is cardinal, and populations not nested by hull can still beat one another in a cycle. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-945](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-945.md) | When each agent's Q-function is approximated as an average of pairwise terms and expanded about the mean action of its neighbours, the first-order term vanishes and the approximation error is a second-order remainder bounded by the curvature of the pairwise Q-function, leaving a two-body problem between an agent and its neighbours' average; with homogeneous agents, mean field Q-learning converges to the Nash Q-value under assumptions the authors call strong, and learned tasks of 500 and 1000 agents where independent and centralized-critic baselines failed | Yang et al. (2018), read in full in [NOTE-1148](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1148.md) from arXiv v5. The expansion and the remainder bound were re-derived when filed; the appendix states an equality where only an inequality holds, which leaves the bound intact. The cancellation of remainders is argued from homogeneity, not proved, and the contraction step needs a high temperature while the convergence theorem assumes a greedy limit. The approximation requires agents interchangeable within a neighbourhood. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-946](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-946.md) | In the zero-sum meta-game on an antisymmetric evaluation matrix the maximum-entropy Nash equilibrium is unique; when the meta-game has only one Nash equilibrium, adding exact copies of an agent splits that agent's mass evenly and leaves every Nash average unchanged; the equilibrium is uniform exactly when every agent's mean log-odds is zero, and uniform on the top-rated agents when the matrix is a pure gradient | Balduzzi et al. (2018), [LIT-1508](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1508.md), Proposition 4, Lemma 1 and Theorem 1, read from arXiv v2 in [NOTE-1155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1155.md), proofs followed. The paper claims invariance to redundant copies without the uniqueness condition. Its proof covers the Nash set, not the maximum-entropy selection. A counterexample checked by script (one copy of a null agent moves an outside agent's Nash average from −0.5 to −0.2) shows the condition is needed. Cardinal: payoffs are log-odds. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-947](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-947.md) | For Blackwell approachability of an approachable polytope under partial monitoring with a known signal law, there are efficient algorithms whose average vector payoff reaches the target at expected distance O(T^-1/3) for general signals and O(T^-1/2) when the signal law does not depend on the decision, the worst-case optimal rates for those two classes | Kwon and Perchet (2017), [LIT-1526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1526.md), read in [NOTE-1159](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1159.md). The rates are for the average payoff's distance to the target, uniformly over Nature's choices, with approachability assumed (Perchet's condition). Optimal means not improvable in the worst case over games. It gives no guarantee for individual stages or rolling windows, and none when the signal law is unknown. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-950](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-950.md) | For a finite partial-monitoring game in which every two actions whose cells meet can estimate their loss difference from their own two signals, RelExp3's expected regret satisfies lim sup E[R_n]/√n ≤ 8√(2K_loc(1+F)(2+F) log K), with K_loc the most actions whose cells share a point and F the number of feedback symbols, and no other game-dependent constant; a two-action game shows that a factor linear in F cannot be avoided in general | Lattimore and Szepesvári (2019), [LIT-1524](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1524.md), read in [NOTE-1162](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1162.md). For the class of games Bartók (2013) studied, the leading constant of the √n regret depends only on K_loc, F and log K, asymptotically. It is the first such result against adversaries. The constant reached before the asymptotics set in still depends on large game constants. It is a bound for one algorithm in a sub-class of the easy games, not a characterisation of the constant. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-957](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-957.md) | When the signal law depends on the decision, Kwon and Perchet's approachability algorithm learns what each decision would reveal only from the stages on which it is played: it keeps every decision's probability at least γ/\|I\| and estimates the flag by importance weighting, an estimate that is conditionally unbiased with second moment Σ_i 1/P[i_t = i] ≤ \|I\|²/γ, with the tuned floor γ shrinking as T^-1/3; when the signal law does not depend on the decision, the raw signal is already unbiased for every component and no floor is used | Kwon and Perchet (2017), [LIT-1526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1526.md), read in [NOTE-1159](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1159.md). Under decision-dependent partial monitoring, information about a decision's signal comes only from playing it, and its unbiased estimate costs variance inversely proportional to the probability of playing it. A floor is how the algorithm keeps that finite. That the floor is necessary in general is supported by the matching lower bound, not shown here. Nothing here says what floor a non-learning system should keep. | Active |
| [THEORY-961](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-961.md) | In a finite partial-monitoring game, an action optimal wherever two neighbouring actions tie has a loss vector on the segment between theirs, so a degenerate or duplicate action never creates a neighbouring pair or decides the trivial class, yet its signals count toward the pair's local observability; and the T^2/3 lower bound for a pair that is not locally observable needs the separating direction in the kernel of the signal matrices of all such actions, not only of the two neighbours | Lattimore and Szepesvári (2019), [LIT-1524](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1524.md), read in [NOTE-1162](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1162.md), on Bartók et al. (2014), [LIT-1528](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1528.md). Of actions optimal only on a boundary: "Although these actions are never uniquely optimal, they can be informative". They enter the classification only through the neighbourhood set N_ab. Bartók et al.'s lower-bound proof chose the separating direction in the kernel of the two neighbours' signals alone. With such an action informative, that direction can be told apart cheaply. The fix is to take it in the kernel of every action in N_ab, which the definition of local observability already provides. It says what such actions contribute, not how often an algorithm must play them. | Active |
| [THEORY-962](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-962.md) v2 | In a finite partial-monitoring game, the signals of a set D of actions determine the expected loss difference of actions i and j under every outcome distribution iff ℓ_i − ℓ_j lies in the sum of the row spaces of their signal matrices; when it does not, two outcome distributions differing along a vector in the common kernel give every action in D the same signal law and reverse the preference between i and j, so no amount of play restricted to D can learn the comparison | Bartók, Foster, Pál, Rakhlin and Szepesvári (2014), [LIT-1528](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1528.md), read in [NOTE-1164](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1164.md). Observability in partial monitoring is a linear-algebra condition on the loss and signal matrices: a comparison is learnable from some actions exactly when its loss difference is in the span of their signal row spaces. Global and local observability are the two choices of D the classification uses. It says what can be estimated, not how fast; the rates are [THEORY-964](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-964.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-963](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-963.md) | The minimax regret of every finite partial-monitoring game against an oblivious adversary, degenerate and duplicate actions included, is 0 when no two actions are neighbours, Θ̃(√n) when every pair of neighbours is locally observable, Θ(n^2/3) when every pair is globally but some pair is not locally observable, and linear otherwise; its lower bounds are proved against stochastic outcomes, so the same four classes hold for them | Lattimore and Szepesvári (2019), [LIT-1524](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1524.md), read in [NOTE-1162](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1162.md), completing Bartók et al. (2014), [LIT-1528](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1528.md). The four classes, trivial, easy, hard and hopeless, now cover every finite game. Two things change from Bartók et al.'s statement: the adversarial half no longer excludes degenerate and duplicate actions, and the trivial class is "no pair of neighbouring actions", not "one non-dominated action", which misplaces games whose extra actions are degenerate or duplicates. It classifies the best policy in a fixed, known game, up to game-dependent constants. It does not cover a learner barred from some actions, feedback that changes during play, or adaptive adversaries. | Active |
| [THEORY-964](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-964.md) v3 | The minimax regret of a finite partial-monitoring game takes one of four rates, decided by its loss and signal matrices: 0 when only one action is non-dominated, Θ̃(√T) when every pair of neighbouring actions is locally observable, Θ(T^2/3) when the game is globally but not locally observable, and Θ(T) when it is not globally observable; against stochastic opponents for every game, against oblivious adversaries for non-degenerate games | Bartók, Foster, Pál, Rakhlin and Szepesvári (2014), [LIT-1528](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1528.md), read in [NOTE-1164](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1164.md). Four classes, trivial, easy, hard and hopeless, with conditions checkable from the matrices before play. It classifies the best policy for a fixed, known game. It does not cover a policy that is barred from some actions, a feedback structure that changes during play, or finite-horizon constants, and its adversarial half excludes degenerate games. | Superseded — by [THEORY-963](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-963.md) |
